subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 22-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department after 24 hours of vomiting and poor oral intake; he is now drowsy and has had a brief generalized seizure. He is afebrile, and his liver edge is slightly enlarged. Laboratory studies show glucose 34 mg/dL, bicarbonate 18 mEq/L, minimal urine ketones, ammonia 95 micrograms/dL, and normal lactate. Plasma acylcarnitine profile shows elevated octanoylcarnitine (C8), and urine contains adipic and suberic acids.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Deficiency of medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase impairs beta-oxidation of medium-chain fatty acids, so fasting produces hypoglycemia with inappropriately low ketones. Medium-chain acylcarnitines (C8) and dicarboxylic acids (adipic, suberic) accumulate, and mild hyperammonemia is common; management is avoidance of fasting and intravenous dextrose during illness.

explanation_incorrect.A: Systemic carnitine deficiency also causes hypoketotic hypoglycemia, but plasma free carnitine is very low and patients typically have muscle weakness and dilated cardiomyopathy rather than an isolated C8 elevation.
explanation_incorrect.B: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I deficiency raises free fatty acids with low ketones and does not produce dicarboxylic aciduria or C8 acylcarnitine elevation.
explanation_incorrect.C: Propionic acidemia causes a ketotic high anion gap acidosis with hyperammonemia and elevated propionylcarnitine (C3), not hypoketosis.
explanation_incorrect.D: HMG-CoA lyase deficiency causes hypoketotic hypoglycemia with metabolic acidosis and elevated 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaric acid, not adipic and suberic acids.

educationalObjective: Hypoketotic hypoglycemia after fasting with elevated C8 acylcarnitine and dicarboxylic aciduria is characteristic of medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency.
